Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test org.apache.commons.math3.fraction.FractionTest.testIntegerOverflow() calls:
- new Fraction(0.75000000001455192, 1.0e-12, 1000)
- new Fraction(1.0e10, 1.0e-12, 1000)
- new Fraction(-1.0e10, 1.0e-12, 1000)
and expects that each call throws a ConvergenceException.

How the bug occurs:
1) The test invokes the constructor Fraction(double, double, int), which delegates to the private constructor Fraction(double, double, int maxDenominator, int maxIterations) with maxDenominator set to Integer.MAX_VALUE.

2) In that private constructor, the first steps are:
   - overflow threshold is set to Integer.MAX_VALUE.
   - a0 = floor(value) is computed.
   - An overflow check is performed only for large positive a0:
     if (a0 > overflow) { throw new FractionConversionException(value, a0, 1l); }

3) For value = 1.0e10:
   - a0 = 10000000000 > Integer.MAX_VALUE, so the above check correctly throws a FractionConversionException (which the test is prepared to accept via catching ConvergenceException).

4) For value ≈ 0.75000000001455192:
   - Continued fraction iteration produces a very large next partial quotient (because the value is extremely close to 3/4). This makes p2 or q2 exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE and the code throws a FractionConversionException at:
     if ((p2 > overflow) || (q2 > overflow)) { throw new FractionConversionException(value, p2, q2); }
   - Again, this is consistent with the test’s expectation.

5) For value = -1.0e10 (the problematic case):
   - a0 = floor(-1.0e10) = -10000000000.
   - The code only checks a0 > overflow (i.e., only for large positive values). It does not check the lower bound (a0 < -overflow) nor the absolute magnitude |a0|.
   - Because -1.0e10 is exactly representable, the “almost-integer” shortcut triggers:
     if (abs(a0 - value) < epsilon) { this.numerator = (int) a0; this.denominator = 1; return; }
   - Here, a0 does not fit into an int. The cast (int) a0 silently overflows, producing an incorrect numerator and, crucially, no exception is thrown.
   - As a result, the test’s try block completes without throwing, and Assert.fail is executed, causing the test to fail.

Why this matches the bug report:
- The current bug report mentions “Fraction(double, int) constructor strange behaviour” with large negative numbers, which is driven by the same private continued-fraction constructor. The underlying issue is asymmetrical overflow handling: only large positive integers are guarded, while large negative integers are not. This leads to silent int overflow when taking the integer shortcut, and can also lead to sign anomalies later in the iteration for other inputs (as noted in the report’s point about positive result from negative input).

Root cause:
- Missing symmetric overflow check for the integer-part a0. The code checks only a0 > Integer.MAX_VALUE, but not a0 < Integer.MIN_VALUE (or equivalently |a0| > Integer.MAX_VALUE).
- The “almost integer” shortcut casts a0 to int without verifying it fits in the int range.

Consequences:
- For negative values whose integer part has magnitude > Integer.MAX_VALUE (e.g., -1e10), the constructor returns a Fraction with a silently overflowed numerator instead of throwing a convergence/overflow exception, violating the test’s expectation.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
